items.question: What led you to think coding agents and custom agents should share the same platform?
items.object: A shared platform for coding agents and custom agents
items.answer:
There were actually a couple of converging lines, which I think is a good sign that you need something new. So, on the one hand, we have a really great dev infra team. They built something called Isaac that lets you use coding agents either on the web in sandboxes or just on your dev machine or on your laptop or whatever. They were adding all kinds of stuff there, and we saw all the more advanced engineers were building their own workflows with tons of agents, and they were building their own UIs and stuff even on top of that.

And then the other one was us building agents. We shipped this data science agent called Genie on the research team, which I co-lead. We also build a lot of internal ones for various things, and then we have all the customer ones, and all of them were running into this thing of, like, oh, I need to switch model and harness and so on every few months. Plus, the agent is completely useless if you can't share sessions with someone and have history and have search and all this layer on top of it for collaboration.

I thought a bit about it from both contexts, and at first people thought it was weird, like, why are you doing coding agents and custom agents in the same thing? But I said it's basically the same problems, and you just want to build the stuff that lets you deliver the agent, maybe control it if you care about security, and make it portable across things. And then we prototyped some things as experiments. We said, yeah, actually we can make it work, and then we built it for real.
quotes: There were actually a couple of converging lines, which I think is a good sign that you need something new.

We have really great dev infra team. items.question: Why do you think protocols and APIs still need to be deliberately designed when people can vibe code software on demand?
items.object: Designed protocols and APIs for interoperability between AI agents, users, and tools
items.answer: So with open sharing, it's like you have a company, you maintain some kind of table, like let's say Walmart or something. They have the inventory and what's been sold in each store. And then you also have suppliers, and they would love to produce more things and ship them exactly the moment you need them. So they would love real-time access to your table. So instead of sending emails around or Excel sheets or phone calls, why can't you share a view of that table in real time with them? Then they query, they join it with their data, and they decide what to send. So it's one of these things where you might ask, like, today since we can vibe code anything so fast, why do we even need to design protocols or APIs or software? Why can't you just vibe code things on demand? But actually, for this type of interoperability where multiple parties that are moving at different speeds are building stuff and you still want some layer on top to coordinate, you do want to design it and build it. So it reminds me of that, agents talking to each other and users talking to agents and tools.

items.question: What do you see as the core value of a common API across agent harnesses such as Claude Code and Codex?
items.object: A common API across agent harnesses
items.answer: I would say the core of this is this common API on top of all the harnesses. So the API is basically like you've got an agent session and you can send in a message or a file. Basically, that's what you can send in, and then you get out these streams as it's streaming text or as it's doing tool calls. Or the other thing you can send in is you can tell it to cancel or turn. So that's the API. Now, the thing we did is we could get you that on top of Claude Code running in a terminal, Codex, Phi, OpenAI SDK, all that stuff. We map them all to that same interface. So that is something that you'd have to maintain yourself if you built your own agent orchestrator. Whenever Claude changes its API, you got to tweak your thing or it's going to lose some messages. So that's the thing that's valuable to maintain. Then on top of that, we built a few apps. I think we built a pretty cool UI and stuff, and we built the security and control piece, which I'm excited about. But it's that common interface. So it doesn't try to be a stack. In fact, you could plug in your own UI on top of this server. That's one of the use cases we care a lot about because we want to use this in our own products.

items.question: Why do you think coding agents need contextual security policies?
items.object: Contextual security policies for coding agents
items.answer: I spent quite a bit of time talking to internal users, developers, security team, managers, and also lots of customers. First of all, one thing that immediately became obvious for security: there's this tension between usability and security. The way people do a lot of coding agents today have very basic things like you can tell me which tool patterns are allowed or disallowed or whatever. It's yes or no. But that puts you in a very tough spot. So, just as an example, should my agent be able to read some confidential documents? Or should it be able to install new packages from NPM, which maybe is compromised? Yes or no. Maybe I want to allow it. Should my agent be able to publish stuff to the company website? Well, if I'm using the code on the website, yes. But should it be able to do both? So it can grab a confidential document and be prompt injected and leak it? Probably not. So, the thing we decided we need is stateful, or what we call contextual policies, where you keep track of the state of that session. It's not like, is it allowed to push to the marketing site or not? But, hey, if it did a risky thing, like it installed a one-day-old package from NPM, or it read a thousand confidential docs, then no. Don't do it. Otherwise, maybe it's okay. That's one example of moving that trade-off. So it's both more secure and more useful by having a more powerful engine, essentially. This requires tracking sessions.

items.question: Why did you design Omnigen's policy layer around functions and libraries?
items.object: Function- and library-based policy design in Omnigen
items.answer: The other piece that was interesting there is there are these very low-level events it's doing, and you want some libraries on top that parse them. For example, we have an MCP server on Google Drive internally. It's got 60 API calls. How do I know which of those will share a document with stuff on the internet and which ones won't? It's annoying. So we designed in Omnigen the policy layer so that it's functions and you can have libraries. Someone can make something that maps the low-level events to high-level ones, and then you write a policy about the high-level things that came out. And that was related to Panther. Panther will help with that. Panther is kind of a similar idea on the event processing side and it's Python based versus a weird custom language. This is sort of more as in real time.

items.question: What do you find valuable about Omnigen's stateful policy design?
items.object: Omnigen's stateful policy design
items.answer: I think the contextual or stateful part, and then the way it can be libraries—these are the cool things. And that was another reason to make it open source, because others will write libraries and we and our customers can use them. And the final thing, because it's stateful, one of the states we track is how much you spent in that session. I've had an agent debug something and it spent $500 because it decided to read a lot of log files and burn a lot of tokens. But I can literally say, “Okay, launch a sub-agent to do this and cap it to spending $5. Ask me for permission if it needs more.” And because we're counting that within that session, it'll pop up and tell me, “Okay, you spent $5. Do you want to go on?”

items.question: Why do you favor L-TAP’s unified storage approach for transactional and analytical workloads?
items.object: L-TAP’s unified storage approach versus HTAP’s single engine
items.answer: A single system that can do both is the holy grail of database engineering. Why not build a single system that can do both? But it ends up being a lot of compromises. One of the first issues is that Postgres has a massive ecosystem. You want to be using the tools built for Postgres. And Spark, for example, had a massive ecosystem. There's a lot of libraries you want to use. If you create a new thing, you don't have an ecosystem. You tend to create a new, smaller, proprietary API, and you're lacking both. It's also very difficult to make it performance-wise comparable on either side. So it ends up sucking at both. Our whole idea of L-TAP is kind of obviously a word play on the term HTAP. HTAP wants to build a single engine for both. We think you can get 99% of what you need by unifying the storage and just having a single storage layer. Once you have the single storage layer, if your Postgres databases are writing data in a column-oriented format, everything analytics can just go read that data directly without any delay. There's no pipeline in between, so all the data would immediately be available for reasoning and analytics.

items.question: What convinced you that unified database storage would be useful for AI agents?
items.object: The usefulness of unified database storage for AI agents
items.answer: I was telling some customers earlier, when we talked about this being super useful for agents, I at first didn't really believe it myself, even though we wrote that positioning. But last night I was having dinner with an Australian customer, and they told me one of the big issues is they have all these logs from their services and see SLA dips and want to investigate. But there's no way for those agents to understand what's going on in the actual databases themselves. All we see is product telemetry of the database and the services. You would make those agents ten times more powerful if you understood, for example, who's actually placing those orders. What is happening? What exactly are they doing? So now I'm actually sold on our own message.

items.question: How do you understand the architectural breakthrough that made L-TAP possible?
items.object: The architectural step from Neon and Lakebase to L-TAP
items.answer: I was talking to somebody at Meta, and he was asking me, “What's the catch? Why is it possible now?” I think the reality is we took a lot of time to actually work on the lake base architecture. Obviously, a lot of it came from the Neon team: separation of storage from compute. It turned out it was just a tiny little step away, going from that to this L-TAP idea. In the Neon architecture and in the lake base architecture, we're writing data in row-oriented format to the open data lake. But in there, we're writing in Postgres pages. Ali and I were spending a lot of time debating, “Can we actually just change that to write in column-oriented format?” We were debating, and then one day one of our engineers, who's actually super smart, came in and said, “I just prototyped it. It works.”

items.question: Why did you decide to focus Databricks’ AI work on making models useful rather than training a general frontier model?
items.object: Databricks’ decision to focus on useful AI systems rather than general frontier models
items.answer: Even though we did launch an open-source model DBRX and went up to above the Llama 3 scale, we decided that there'll be so many people releasing models. Instead of doing the general model, where a big part of the recipe is just throwing a lot of compute and scale, we want to focus on the next step: let's say you have the very smart model, how do you make it useful? For us it was a lot about automating, making it very good at querying data. That's the first-party agent we have called Genie. It's like a virtual data scientist. Imagine there's someone who already knows all the stuff in your company inside out and knows all the machine learning libraries, all the data libraries, all the stuff on the web, and you can ask them questions. That's what we wanted to do first. So that meant let's not focus as much on training some kind of frontier model, but let's build a system using either external models or fine-tuned customized components.

items.question: Where do you see specialized models offering an advantage over general frontier models?
items.object: Specialized models for high-volume tasks such as document parsing
items.answer: We're still doing quite a bit of model training, though. We're procuring lots of GPUs all the time to do it. There are a few places where we're doing that. One is many high-volume use cases where, if you have a specialized model, it's so much better than any of the general models you get. A nice example is understanding documents, like PDF, Word documents, parsing them. If you've ever tried to do that, it's frustrating because you send it to Claude or whatever, it almost gets it, but it gets some things wrong. And it's super expensive. You just burned a huge amount of tokens plopping in an image. Our team built a document vision model that takes a page and gives you back a nice JSON with all the components. It's very competitive. It's probably 100x cheaper than those frontier models and still better. That's done by one of the researchers who came from DeepMind, was a co-founder of Adapt, a very early LLM scaling person, but focused on this. Likewise, we're doing specialized sub-agents for part of what the coding agent does.
